chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man: is it proper for him to recite in his salat (prayer) and move his tongue with the recitation in his throat without making himself hear it? He said: There is no problem if he does not move his tongue, and merely imagines it inwardly.

So the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as applying to one who prays behind someone who is not to be followed; it is permissible for him to recite within himself, like inner self-talk. This indicates that.

key_terms.حَدِيثِ النَّفْسِ: inner self-talk, used here to describe inaudible internal recitation
key_terms.خَلْفَ: behind, referring to praying behind another leader in salat (prayer)
key_terms.صَلَاتِهِ: his salat (prayer), the ritual act under discussion
key_terms.لَا يُقْتَدَى بِهِ: one who is not followed as an Imam in prayer
key_terms.لِسَانَهُ: his tongue, referring to physical articulation in recitation
key_terms.يَتَوَهَّمُ: he imagines inwardly, indicating silent internal recitation
key_terms.يُسْمِعَ نَفْسَهُ: make himself hear, meaning audible recitation to oneself

ai.seo_question: Can a person recite silently in salat (prayer) without making himself hear the recitation?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling of recitation in salat (prayer), particularly whether one must audibly hear oneself or may recite inwardly. The concluding note explains that the report is interpreted as referring to someone praying behind an Imam who is not to be followed, in which case inward recitation like inner speech is allowed.
